verdict: Caution: lend selectively to cumin processors and exporters with hedged stock and clean receivables; avoid pure mandi traders and unhedged stock financiers until price and export signals settle.
title: Unjha Spices Processing & Trade: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
Unjha is Asia's largest cumin market, so the town's cash engine is jeera: arrival, grading, cleaning, grinding and export [3]. **The borrower buys raw jeera at harvest, holds stock, processes and sells into domestic and export channels.** Value sits in grading and cleaning quality and in the export relationship, not in the raw seed itself. Cost is dominated by raw material; ICRA notes raw material is the largest cost component for FMCG players [11]. Working capital is heavy: ICRA flags NWC/OI of around 45% as on March 31, 2025 for a peer, improved from 51% in FY2024, with seasonal raw material availability February to June forcing higher stock [9]. So when a proposal lands, check the stock-and-receivable cycle against the February-June buying window; if stock is held past the selling season without a buyer contract, ask for the offtake evidence.

## What has changed now
Local news is firm: Unjha mandi strengthened with steady exports [1], and a Gujarati report cites a single-session jump of ₹1,200 in jeera on El Niño fear [2]. **That is a price-led rally, not a volume story, and price rallies flatter trader turnover while hiding stock risk.** Peer results show the same pattern: Orkla India's Q1 revenue rose 10.4% with pricing contributing 11.4%, while chilli and coriander inflation climbed 78% and 40% [6]. Nationally, exports are down 5.7% Apr-to-date in USD [D], so export-dependent Unjha buyers face softer overseas pull even as local prices firm. Gujarat GST collections are up 11.9% Apr-to-date versus India's 6.1% [D], a genuine local tailwind. Note the local sources are recent (Oct 2026) but thin on Unjha-specific credit data; the rating reports are undated, so treat them as structural, not current.

## Where to grow
**Pursue processors and exporters with branded or contracted offtake, and second-stage units adding grinding and packing capacity.** Peer evidence supports demand: Orkla India's spices volumes surged over 10% [4], and its international business is around 21% of revenues across 45 countries [5]. Pursue borrowers with a UAE or Gulf channel, since Eastern is the No. 1 Indian spice brand in the UAE by household reach [5]. Avoid pure mandi traders who finance stock on price expectation, and avoid anyone whose repayment depends on the ₹1,200 rally holding [2].

## How to grow safely
Structure against the stock, not the story. **Take monthly stock statements, ageing of receivables and a margined drawing power tied to realisable jeera value, not the peak mandi print.** Ask for export order copies and shipping bills where export is claimed, given the 5.7% national export decline [D]. ICRA notes utilisation is typically higher July-November, till Diwali [10], so size limits to the peak season and require deleveraging after it. Collect from customer: actual stock turnover days, export share of sales, and hedging policy.

## Early-warning signs
- Weekly mandi price versus borrower's booked stock value: a fall of the kind that reversed the ₹1,200 spike [2] -> revalue drawing power and call for margin.
- Monthly export order book and shipping bills: two months of falling orders against the 5.7% national export decline [D] -> freeze fresh limits.
- Monthly stock statement: stock ageing beyond the February-June procurement norm [9] -> demand sale or additional collateral.
- Quarterly GST filings: divergence from Gujarat's 11.9% growth [D] -> investigate sales suppression.
